\section[el reto]{el reto — the challenge}

\label{lesson:ES-C766-reto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for imagination, then the Spanish for to aspire.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el reto}
\textbf{el reto} — \textquotedblleft{}the challenge\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Aprender chino es un gran reto.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Learning Chinese is a big challenge.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Desafío} is a synonym.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{reto} is built on \emph{retar} (EtymDB), which comes from Old French \emph{reter} \textquotedblleft{}to accuse\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{reputāre} \textquotedblleft{}to reckon\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el reto}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el reto}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for imagination, then the Spanish for to aspire, then say \emph{el reto} again
\end{itemize}

\section[la ambición]{la ambición — ambition}

\label{lesson:ES-C766-ambicion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to aspire, then the Spanish for the challenge.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la ambición}
\textbf{la ambición} — \textquotedblleft{}ambition\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Su ambición es abrir un restaurante.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Her ambition is to open a restaurant.}
\end{quote}

It can be positive or negative.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ambición} comes from Latin \emph{ambitiō} \textquotedblleft{}a going round, canvassing\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{ambīre} \textquotedblleft{}to go around\textquotedblright{}: a Roman candidate went round asking for votes.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la ambición}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la ambición}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to aspire, then the Spanish for the challenge, then say \emph{la ambición} again
\end{itemize}

\section[creativo]{creativo — creative}

\label{lesson:ES-C766-creativo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the challenge, then the Spanish for ambition.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: creativo}
\textbf{creativo} — \textquotedblleft{}creative\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Es una persona muy creativa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She is a very creative person.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Un creativo} also means someone who works in advertising.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{creativo} is a learned borrowing from Late Latin \emph{creātīvus} (EtymDB), built on \emph{creāre} \textquotedblleft{}to create\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[el logro]{el logro — the achievement}

\label{lesson:ES-C766-logro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for ambition, then the Spanish for creative.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el logro}
\textbf{el logro} — \textquotedblleft{}the achievement\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Terminar la carrera fue un gran logro.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Finishing my degree was a great achievement.}
\end{quote}

The verb is \emph{lograr}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{logro} comes from Latin \emph{lucrum} \textquotedblleft{}gain, profit\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), through \emph{lograr}, from \emph{lucrārī} \textquotedblleft{}to gain\textquotedblright{}; in old Spanish \emph{logro} also meant interest on a loan.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el talento]{el talento — talent}

\label{lesson:ES-C766-talento}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for creative, then the Spanish for the achievement.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el talento}
\textbf{el talento} — \textquotedblleft{}talent\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tiene mucho talento para la música.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She has a great talent for music.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{talento} was borrowed from Latin \emph{talentum}, from Greek \emph{tálanton} \textquotedblleft{}a balance, a weight of silver\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); the parable of the talents turned money into gifts.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
